page_intro: Most of this lab's work concerns a condition that takes away people's ability to walk comfortably and gets remarkably little attention for how common it is. Around that we have built the two kinds of evidence needed to study anything properly: what happens to very large numbers of real patients, and what happens mechanically inside a single hip.
a1_p1: The gluteus medius and minimus sit on the side of the hip and hold the pelvis level every time you stand on one leg, which is to say with every step you take. When their tendons degenerate or tear, walking becomes a limp, stairs become difficult, and sleep is usually the first thing to go, because the painful side is the side you lie on. It affects roughly one in six adults over 50 and falls disproportionately on women in their fifties and sixties, most of whom are told they have bursitis, given a steroid injection, and sent away. The tendon is usually the real problem, and if it goes unrecognised long enough the muscle is replaced by fat, which does not reverse. By then the options narrow. Anti-inflammatory drugs are risky on older kidneys, so pain that never resolves drifts toward stronger medication. Some patients are offered a hip replacement that was never going to help, because the joint was not the thing that hurt. And even a sound repair may return only a fraction of the function the patient was expecting.
a1_p2: Our work is an attempt to build the missing evidence base from the ground up. We started by collecting every published description of the lesion, nine studies using competing acronyms, and reconciling them into a single account of what is actually being described. We are asking who develops it, using a cohort of 385,868 women to test whether hormone therapy after menopause changes the risk and whether the timing of starting it matters. We assessed every outcome instrument used in these patients against formal measurement standards, since most were designed for hip replacement rather than tendon repair, and we are testing which MRI findings predict which parts of recovery rather than recovery in general. We pooled the treatment literature, from physical therapy through injections to open and endoscopic repair, into one staged pathway. The end of it is a consensus process with radiologists, primary care physicians, and physical therapists to settle the naming and the diagnostic criteria for the field rather than for one group. Once a disease can be named and counted, it can be studied properly, funded, and eventually paid for.
a2_p1: Most questions in orthopaedics never get a randomized trial. The conditions are too uncommon, the outcomes take a decade to appear, and a trial large enough to answer the question would cost more than anyone will pay, so surgeons fall back on experience and on studies of a few hundred patients from a single hospital. There is a second limitation that gets less attention. A trial reports an average. If a treatment helps one group of patients a great deal and does nothing for everyone else, the average comes out small and the treatment is written off. That is not a statistical curiosity. It means something that would have worked for a definable group of people is abandoned for all of them, and nobody ever finds out who they were.
a2_p2: Health records now cover tens of millions of patients, which is enough to reach questions a trial cannot. The difficulty is that this data was produced by care rather than by research, so it is full of traps: patients who look healthier because they were selected for treatment, follow-up that simply stops when someone changes insurer, and associations that reflect referral patterns rather than biology. A good part of the work is controlling those problems well enough that the answer means something. We use these networks to screen dozens of medications at once for association with arthritis, to compare how implants survive in patients with cerebral palsy or multiple sclerosis against patients with ordinary arthritis, to link databases that have not previously been combined, and to measure what care costs from the bottom up rather than accepting the hospital's accounting. The same records let us test other people's work: journals publish machine learning models constantly and very few are ever run on data from another hospital, so we check which survive contact with an outside dataset and what separates those that do. Assembling a cohort from messy records used to take months of manual chart review, and we build and audit software agents to do that work in a form we can check.
a3_p1: A surgeon repairing a torn tendon decides how many anchors to use, where to place them, and whether to reinforce the repair with a graft or a synthetic patch. Those decisions are mechanical, and they are mostly made by feel, because there is no way to try them on the patient in front of you. Repairs of the hip abductors fail often enough to matter, and a failed repair is not a neutral event: it means a second operation on tissue that was already damaged, after a year of rehabilitation that returned the patient to roughly where they started. The same gap between judgement and measurement shows up in knee replacement. Hundreds of thousands are done in the United States every year, and around one in five of those patients is still dissatisfied afterwards, a figure that has barely moved in twenty years, usually blamed on a knee that was not balanced quite right.
a3_p2: We build computer models of individual patients from scans they have already had, so the geometry, the tear, and the state of the muscle belong to that person rather than to an average. The model shows where load concentrates and which part of a construct is carrying it, which is usually where a repair begins to fail. Because a simulation is only as good as its assumptions, we test the same constructs in cadaveric tissue, which is harder than it sounds: the muscle tears out of the clamp before the repair itself does, so measuring the strength of a repair means first solving the problem of holding onto the muscle. The third way to study mechanics is to measure them during the operation itself. A robotic system plans every cut before the first incision and then records what was actually measured once the surgeon is inside the joint, and almost none of that record is ever examined afterwards. We treat the plan as a prediction and check it against what the surgeon found. It underestimates the gap on the inner side of the knee, and the error grows the more bowed the leg was to begin with, which a surgeon can correct for once they know it is there.

open_problems.title: Predicting which abductor tendon repairs fail
open_problems.desc: Gluteus medius repairs fail at meaningful rates, and outcomes vary widely. Using imaging, intraoperative findings, and longitudinal outcomes from our repair cohort, the goal is a model that identifies repairs at high risk of failure and the factors that drive it.
open_problems.needs: Data: imaging, operative, outcomes · Methods: ML, survival analysis

open_problems.title: From intraoperative data to a structured operative record
open_problems.desc: Robotic platforms log detailed data for every case, but little of it reaches surgical registries because the translation is manual. The problem is an agentic pipeline that converts intraoperative and EHR data into structured, auditable documentation a surgeon would sign.
open_problems.needs: Data: robotic logs, EHR · Methods: LLM agents, FHIR

open_problems.title: Separating cause from association in drug-osteoarthritis screens
open_problems.desc: A medication-wide screen surfaces many drugs associated with osteoarthritis. Association is not cause. The work is to take the strongest signals and test them with negative controls, target-trial emulation, and sensitivity analysis to see what holds.
open_problems.needs: Data: federated EHR · Methods: causal inference, pharmacoepidemiology

open_problems.title: A fast surrogate for patient-specific finite element analysis
open_problems.desc: A full finite element model of a repair construct takes hours to build and solve. A learned surrogate that predicts the stress field from imaging in seconds, accurately enough to inform a decision, would make this usable in clinic.
open_problems.needs: Data: imaging, FE models · Methods: surrogate modeling, geometry processing

open_problems.title: Correcting the robot's gap prediction across deformity
open_problems.desc: Robotic knee replacement underpredicts the medial gap as native coronal deformity increases. The problem is to characterize that error across the full deformity range and build a correction a surgeon can use intraoperatively.
open_problems.needs: Data: robotic arthroplasty · Methods: modeling, data science

open_problems.title: A reproducible classification for concealed abductor tears
open_problems.desc: Undersurface abductor tears sit beneath intact superficial fibers and are described in the literature under competing names. The work is an imaging-based, reproducible classification, ideally with automated segmentation, that the field can use consistently.
open_problems.needs: Data: MRI · Methods: segmentation, clinical research
